claim:mw-equilibrium-reproduction.proposition: Reproducing the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium: rate crossing + turnover
claim:mw-equilibrium-reproduction.hypothesis:
The mw_equilibrium composite colonizes each absent species at probability
c = colonization_base/(1+distance) and goes extinct each present species at
e = extinction_base*(ref_area/area)^area_exponent. Immigration I(S)=(P-S)c
falls with S, extinction E(S)=S*e rises with S, so richness must relax to and
fluctuate about S* = P*c/(c+e). Because colonization and extinction never stop,
the island keeps gaining and losing species at equilibrium (turnover), so gross
colonization+extinction events over a window vastly exceed the net change in S.

provenance.note:
Measured eq_track_corr = 0.992 (12 islands, 8-seed ensemble, 400
generations, tail 25%). 0.9 is a conservative floor for "tracks theory".

Measured turnover_ratio = 15.5 on the representative mid-gradient island
(gross colonization+extinction / |net dS| over the tail window).

claim:species-area-and-isolation.proposition: The species-area law and the isolation gradient
claim:species-area-and-isolation.hypothesis:
In the extinction-limited regime, S* ~ A^(area_exponent), so a log-spaced area
gradient at fixed isolation should give a straight line on log-log axes with
slope z ~ area_exponent. Separately, because colonization c = c0/(1+distance)
falls hyperbolically with distance, a distance gradient at fixed area should
give richness that drops steeply then plateaus — a monotone decline (rank
correlation strongly negative).

provenance.note:
Measured z = 0.12 (area gradient 1-100, isolation 0, 8-seed ensemble).
Within the low end of the empirical 0.1-0.35 band; large islands approach
pool saturation, which flattens the slope.

Measured Spearman = -0.97 (distance gradient 0-30 at fixed area 30,
8-seed ensemble). Pearson is only -0.79 because the c=c0/(1+d) decline is
hyperbolic; rank correlation captures the monotonicity.

claim:neutral-vs-equilibrium.proposition: Neutral vs equilibrium: do dispersal-drift and colonization-extinction predict the same macroecology?
claim:neutral-vs-equilibrium.hypothesis:
The neutral metacommunity (Hubbell 2001) holds a zero-sum local community of
J = area*density individuals evolving by J Moran death/replacement events per
generation, with immigration probability m = immigration_base/(1+distance) from
a shared pool of n_pool species. Larger islands sample and retain more species
before drift erodes them, so a positive species-area relationship must emerge
with NO colonization/extinction rate asymmetry at all — purely from drift plus
dispersal. Run alongside the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium composite over the
same area gradient, both models should show a positive z, but by different
mechanisms and (potentially) with different slopes. The neutral local community
should also display the characteristic skewed, concave rank-abundance /
zero-sum-multinomial species-abundance distribution from drift alone.

provenance.note:
Measured z_neutral = 0.763 (12 islands log-spaced area 1-100, density 2
→ J 2-200, immigration_base 0.2, n_pool 64, 8-seed ensemble, 300
generations, tail 25%). 0.05 is a conservative floor for "clear positive
SAR"; the measured value is far above it.

Measured z_neutral = 0.763 and z_equilibrium = 0.126 over the identical
area gradient (MacArthur-Wilson composite, n_pool 60, colonization_base
0.02, extinction_base 0.012, area_exponent 0.25). Both exceed 0.05, so
both_sar = 1.0 (both-positive indicator).

claim:microbial-island-biogeography.proposition: Does the taxa-area relationship hold for microbes — and flatten?
claim:microbial-island-biogeography.hypothesis:
Microbial communities obey the same equilibrium logic as macro-organisms
(richness set by the crossing of area-driven extinction against isolation-
driven colonization), so a microbial regime should still give a positive
taxa-area slope (z > 0). But because microbes draw on an enormous taxa pool
(so islands rarely saturate), disperse widely, and turn over fast locally
(martiny2006microbial; hanson2012beyond), the area effect on extinction is
weaker and the measured slope should be *flatter* than the macro slope —
consistent with the observed microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1 (hornerdevine2004taxa;
bell2005islands) versus the classic macro z ~ 0.15-0.35.

provenance.note:
Measured z_micro = 0.0429 (area gradient 1-100, isolation 0, 6-seed
ensemble; microbial regime n_pool=300, colonization_base=0.10,
extinction_base=0.06, area_exponent=0.10). Positive and squarely inside
the empirical microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1 (hornerdevine2004taxa salt-
marsh sediment; bell2005islands tree-hole bacteria).

Measured z_micro = 0.0429 vs z_macro = 0.1227 over the identical area
gradient and seeds (6-seed ensemble), so z_flatter_margin =
z_macro - z_micro = 0.0798 > 0. z_macro reproduces the 0.12 slope the
species-area-and-isolation study measured in the macro regime. The
microbial slope is ~2.9x flatter, consistent with the observed microbe-
vs-macro contrast (hornerdevine2004taxa; hanson2012beyond). Gross
equilibrium turnover is ~20x higher in the microbial regime (25.99 vs
1.27 events · gen⁻¹ · island⁻¹), the fast-turnover signature.

claim:general-dynamic-model.proposition: General Dynamic Model: does island ontogeny make richness hump then decline?
claim:general-dynamic-model.hypothesis:
The GeneralDynamicModelProcess uses the same colonization/extinction
bookkeeping as the MacArthur-Wilson process — each of n_pool mainland species
present or absent, colonizing absent species at c = colonization_base and
removing present species at e(t) — but recomputes e(t) each tick from a
time-varying area(t) = area_max*((t/t_peak)*exp(1-t/t_peak))^ontogeny_shape
that rises to area_max at t_peak then erodes. Because extinction falls with
area, the instantaneous equilibrium S*(t) = P*c/(c+e(t)) is itself humped.
Richness chases this moving target with a relaxation lag, so it must rise to an
overshoot while the island is young and large, then decline as the island
erodes — a hump the static MacArthur-Wilson plateau cannot produce. The lag
also makes the richness-vs-area trajectory trace a hysteresis loop (richness
peaks after area and decays more slowly).

provenance.note:
Measured on the focal mid-age island (island_01, t_peak=150), 10-seed
ensemble, 500 model-time units (run length 501 ticks; middle third =
ticks 167-334). Ensemble-mean richness peaks at S = 51.8 at t = 195
(well inside the middle third), rising from an early-run mean of 18.5
(first 10%) and falling to a late-run mean of 26.7 (last 10%) — a
peak/late ratio of 1.94 and peak/early of 2.80. Both ends clear the
0.75*peak = 38.9 margin, so the hump gate passes with room to spare. The
0.75 margin and middle-third window are conservative floors for a visible
overshoot-then-decline.

claim:rescue-effect.proposition: The rescue effect: immigration lowers extinction (Brown & Kodric-Brown 1977)
claim:rescue-effect.hypothesis:
If the same colonization pressure c that fills empty niches also rescues
present species (each present species rescued per tick with probability c, its
extinction probability then cut to e*(1-rescue_strength)), the effective
per-species extinction rate becomes e_eff = e*(1 - c*rescue_strength). The
extinction curve is pulled down, so the rate crossing slides right: equilibrium
richness rises to S* = P*c/(c + e*(1-c*rescue_strength)) and the equilibrium
event flux S*·e_eff — the turnover — falls. With rescue_strength=0 the model
reduces exactly to the independent-curves MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium.

provenance.note:
Measured S = 37.26 at r=0.8 vs 30.10 at r=0 (margin +7.16 species;
9-island rescue gradient, 8-seed ensemble, 400 generations, tail 25%,
c=e=0.5, P=60). The simulated gradient tracks the analytic
S*(r)=P*c/(c+e(1-c*r)) across all levels (30.00 -> 37.50). 2.0 is a
conservative floor for "clearly more species".

Measured equilibrium turnover 30.02 events/gen at r=0 vs 22.56 at r=0.8
(drop 7.45 events/gen; turnover ratio 0.752), same ensemble. Turnover
falls monotonically along the rescue gradient. 2.0 is a conservative
floor for a clear reduction.

claim:island-archipelago.proposition: Carrying capacity sets abundance, not richness
claim:island-archipelago.hypothesis:
Area enters the model only through the carrying capacity
(max_individuals_capacity = area * individuals_per_area), which caps TOTAL
individuals. With a random (non-trophic) interaction matrix, Lotka-Volterra
competition drives strong competitive exclusion on every island regardless of
size, so equilibrium TOTAL ABUNDANCE should scale tightly with area while
equilibrium SPECIES RICHNESS should be low and essentially independent of area
— i.e. this model does NOT reproduce the classic MacArthur-Wilson species-area
law under random competition.

provenance.note:
Carrying capacity is area * individuals_per_area and the LV rescale
drives each island's total to that cap; the ~1.00 correlation is a
direct, near-deterministic consequence of the ported update rule.

Measured richness-vs-log-area corr under random competition is ~ -0.10
(6-island, 30-species, seed 0, equilibrium tail); 0.35 is a generous
ceiling that still fails loudly if a strong positive species-area law
appeared, which it does not for non-trophic interactions.

claim:distance-immigration.proposition: Isolation reduces colonization; migration conserves individuals
claim:distance-immigration.hypothesis:
Because the per-pair migration probability falls as 1/(1+distance), an island
that is on average farther from the others should receive fewer immigrants per
generation, so immigration received should correlate negatively with mean
distance. Separately, every emigration moves exactly one individual to exactly
one other island, so the archipelago-wide net migration flux must be exactly
zero (individuals are conserved by the coupler).

provenance.note:
Measured ~ -0.7 to -0.74 (8-island geometry, full-occupancy tally,
seed ensemble). -0.3 is a conservative negative ceiling.

Conservation is exact by construction: each migration event writes -1 to
the source and +1 to the destination of the same species.

claim:island-food-web.proposition: Trophic structure restores the species-area law
claim:island-food-web.hypothesis:
Antisymmetric predator-prey interactions stabilise coexistence (a predator's
gain is its prey's loss, so no single species runs away), so larger islands —
with more carrying capacity to support more trophic links — should sustain
MORE species. The food-web variant should therefore show a POSITIVE
richness-vs-area correlation (recovering the MacArthur-Wilson species-area law)
and support higher equilibrium richness than the random-competition archipelago
of Study 1 at matched parameters.

provenance.note:
Measured ~ +0.50 (8-island, 30-species, 6-seed ensemble, 150
generations). 0.2 is a conservative positive floor that still fails if
the species-area signal collapsed.

Measured gain ~ +1.8 species (food web ~3.8 vs random ~1.95, matched
params). The ordering — not an exact gap — is the falsifiable signature.

narrative.question:
Does island biogeography theory — MacArthur & Wilson's equilibrium of
immigration and extinction (1963, 1967) — hold up when built as composable
process-bigraph models, and where does it bend? Three layers: (1) reproduce
the ORIGINAL theory directly (the colonization/extinction rate model), (2) ask
how much of it a faithful Lotka-Volterra metacommunity port reproduces and why,
and (3) extend it with four nuanced follow-ups — neutral theory, microbial
ecology, island ontogeny, and the rescue effect.
